title: Kernel divergence & CUDA-graph debugging: TRT-LLM vs vLLM runaway paths
summary: Deep dive to investigate intermittent tail-latency spikes and kernel-choice divergence when using CUDA graphs with TRT-LLM vs vLLM on on-prem NVLink cluster. Covered KV cache interactions, quantized path behavior, and VPC/on-prem constraints for debugging traces.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-06-14 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Lina G, Ethan M, Priya N; Marco R, Jenny C, Derek H
Links shared: perf traces Dropbox: https://redwood.share/atlasgrid-traces, deck: https://redwood.example.com/decks/kernel-debug

[00:00] Lina (AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, i think we have about an hour, quick intro — im lina from redwood, ethan is our performance se, priya is infra pm. marco, jenny, derek, do you want to do a one-liner on what you've seen?
[00:17] Marco (ML Eng): yeah sure — thanks, we've been seeing these tail spikes on our onprem cluster when using cudagraphs. small batch, like 1 to 4, latency is great usually but once every few hundred requests we see a 400 to 800 ms jump. looks related to kernel selection switching during graph replay, and it seems different between trt-llm and vllm runs.
[00:34] Jenny (SRE): and to add, the issue is worse after periods of inactivity or when inference memory is under pressure — kv cache eviction maybe. we also run quantized int8 for cost.
[00:52] Ethan (SE): ok good context. quick clarifying q: your onprem nodes are NVLink-connected 8x A100s with local NFS model storage and k8s, right?
[01:07] Derek (CTO): correct, NVLink, k8s (open to using our private operator), models mounted via NFS. we have KMS via cloud HSM, and because of compliance some traces cannot leave the VPC — you may get truncated traces from us.
[01:24] Priya (Infra PM): noted — we can work with masked traces. quick note: when you say trt-llm, are you using the TRT-LLM kernel pack with cuda-graph capture enabled and static shapes?
[01:37] Marco: yes, capture + replay. shapes are dynamic but we do shape-specialization before capture in most flows. sometimes we fall back to non-graph path when a mismatch occurs.
[01:52] Ethan: cool. ok, lets walk through recorded traces. i pulled the trace set you uploaded. first observation, we see two distinct kernel families selected on replay: a fused attention kernel (we'll call K_fuse) vs a fallback multi-kernel attention (K_split). the microsecond delta is small in isolation but the scheduler hiccups cause queuing that amplifies into the 400ms tail spike.
[02:15] Marco: can you show where the decision happens? is it a runtime kernel selection based on sequence length or kv cache state?
[02:27] Ethan: mostly architecture + sequence length heuristics, but we also saw an input dependent branch triggered by the kv cache size — if the kv cache doesn't fit preferred tile sizes, the kernel selector picks a different algo. the cudagraph replay sometimes records the chosen kernels but on rebind at replay time the selector can choose a different kernel if the allocator layout changed.
[02:50] Jenny: thats consistent with our theory — after long pauses the allocator fragmentation is different, and replay rebind picks K_split.
[03:05] Lina (AE): couple of questions for prioritization: does this cause correctness problems? or mostly latency?
[03:12] Marco: only latency, outputs are the same. correctness is stable across both kernels.
[03:18] Ethan: we also profiled TRT-LLM vs vLLM. vLLM tends to prefer streamed kernels with smaller memory footprint, so it avoids switching in some cases. TRT-LLM favors heavy fused kernels that are high throughput but brittle when memory layout shifts during cudagraph rebind.
[03:38] Derek: hmm so trt-llm gives you a big perf win normally but is less resilient to env jitter
[03:45] Ethan: exactly.
[03:47] [04:00] Speaker 3 (incorrectly labeled): we should also check quant path — int8 quantization sometimes alters tiling and produces different kernel choices.
[04:12] Marco: yes, we only started seeing the spikes after switching to int8 with asymmetric calibration. before quant it was stable.
[04:21] Ethan: that matches. int8 reduces precision but changes conv/attention micro-kernels used. the kernel mapper has heuristics that prefer certain tile sizes for int8 which are more sensitive to memory placement. with cuda graphs, the capture stores kernel instances by function pointer and shape; upon replay, if the allocator returns a different pointer the binder can mismatch and force a different path.
[04:45] Jenny: is that a bug or expected behavior? can you pin allocators?
[04:50] Priya: you can reserve a pinned arena to stabilize addresses; we recommend a persistent allocator for cudagraph heavy workloads. also, enabling prefetch for kv cache reduces eviction thrashing.
[05:05] Marco: we looked at persistent allocators but worried about overall memory pressure and multi-tenant oversubscription on our k8s nodes.
[05:14] Ethan: tradeoff indeed. we discussed a few mitigations: 1) persistent arena to stabilize kernel pointers, 2) KV cache prefetch and soft-eviction thresholds to avoid layout churn, 3) fallback policy to do a quick warmup run before capture so memory layout stabilizes.
[05:34] Lina: can you run a repro with and without persistent allocator and share the traces? we'll compare kernel families and timestamps.
[05:42] Marco: yes we can — but note our traces contain secrets, we need redacted traces.
[05:48] Lina: fine, use the redwood masked-trace script we shared.
[05:55] Ethan: another observation: cudagraph replay interacts poorly with lazy kernel compilation in trt-llm. if the first capture triggers compilation of JIT kernels and later replays run a slightly different codegen (e.g., different unrolling for int8), you can get different performance. vLLM's path tends to do more stable JIT decisions at init.
[06:20] Marco: so the fix could be forcing eager compilation before capture?
[06:27] Ethan: yeah 'eager compile' is a good test. also fix the codegen flags to be deterministic.
[06:33] Jenny: any quick wins that don't require code changes?
[06:36] Ethan: persistent allocator + small warmup + pin nvlink mapping for large tensors is all config-level. also disable cudagraph capture for sequences with high shape variance.
[06:50] Derek: important for us: we prefer not to alter app-level logic if possible, ops teams want config levers only. is there a safe default?
[06:58] Lina: we have a recommended config for on-prem: persistent arena=true, kv prefetch=on, cudagraph threshold=stable-shape-only, quant calibration enforced symmetric. we'll share that doc.
[07:14] Marco: you mentioned kv prefetch — how aggressive should that be? we saw more memory pressure when prefetching every request.
[07:23] Ethan: tune the prefetch window to recent active prefixes and cap total prefetched tokens per model instance — e.g., prefetch up to 4 recent prompts with LRU eviction. that reduces cold-start misses but avoids bloat.
[07:40] [08:00] Marco: i want to dig deeper into the profiler output you shared. at 00:42 trace there's a spike where the kernel queue length jumps. can you explain what the trace markers mean?
[08:10] Ethan: sure. trace marker TF0 is kernel enqueue, TF1 is cudagraph begin, TF2 is replay bind. the spike is between TF1 and TF2 when the binder walks the allocator map and selects kernels; if binder chooses K_split it inserts more kernel launches which causes queue saturation.
[08:36] Marco: any way to make binder deterministic?
[08:40] Ethan: long-term we want deterministic binder state — deterministic codegen + address-invariant kernel lookup. short term, persistent allocator plus capturing a warmup trace locks in choices.
[08:52] Jenny: is there any impact from our networked model storage (NFS)? sometimes the mmap addresses differ after remounts.
[08:58] Priya: yes, remount can change addresses. we recommend local model copy or ensure remounts are avoided during runtime. also disable lazy unload of model segments.
[09:12] Marco: good call — we'll test local copy.
[09:16] Ethan: also a note on telemetry: we saw a correlation between hostside memory fragmentation and kernel divergence. if your OS is doing heavy page reclamation during GC pause, allocators shift. consider cgroup mem settings to limit page reclaim.
[09:36] [10:00] Derek: can redwood provide a minimal repro we can run with our operator? even a small docker image that toggles allocator mode?
[10:10] Lina: yes we can provide a repro harness and a benchmark script (we'll attach in follow-up).
[10:15] Marco: thanks. question: we operate behind strict VPC egress rules — how feasible is sending full nvidia-nsight traces?
[10:24] Priya: we can send masked events; also redwood can provide an on-prem agent to upload traces to our secure s3 endpoint.
[10:33] Lina: we'll send a redwood agent tarball that runs inside your VPC and uploads to your S3. agent will redact PII and keys.
[10:40] Jenny: good. another item — are there any known incompatibilities with our HSM KMS setup? we've had issues with session tokens expiring and causing cold starts.
[10:49] Ethan: that can cause cold-start spikes but shouldn't change kernel choice. it creates a different cause of latency: repeated model reloads causing allocator churn. longer-term we recommend session caching for HSM keys or a KMS proxy.
[11:05] Marco: circling back to quant — is there a recommended calibration approach to avoid kernel divergence?
[11:10] Ethan: use symmetric calibration and align per-layer scales. also prefer per-channel quant for attention matrices where possible; it reduces odd tiling choices.
[11:22] [11:40] Marco: can you list the exact config toggles we should try in order?
[11:25] Lina: sure — 1) persistent allocator=true; 2) kv cache prefetch small window (2-4); 3) eager compile before capture; 4) disable cudagraph for high-variance shapes; 5) symmetric int8 calibration; 6) local model copy (avoid remounts); 7) cap tenant memory to reduce host-side fragmentation.
[11:47] Derek: sounds good. time check — we have like 15 minutes left, any deep profiler demos?
[11:55] Ethan: i'll share two trace overlays: one where cudagraph replay kept K_fuse and one where binder picked K_split. you can see the enqueue latency diff. i'll also attach nvtx slices and the binder decision table.
[12:10] Marco: perfect. any idea on expected reduction of spikes with those changes?
[12:15] Ethan: with persistent allocator + kv prefetch + eager compile we typically see spike rate drop by 90% in our lab runs; still a few outliers remain until codegen determinism is enforced.
[12:29] Lina: ok let's capture next steps and owners.
[12:34] [12:40] CROSSTALK: (laughter)
[12:41] Jenny: one more Q — if we switch to vLLM for a pilot, do we lose throughput? what's the tradeoff?
[12:48] Ethan: vLLM tends to be steadier for low-latency small-batch use-cases; TRT-LLM has higher peak throughput at larger batch sizes. for your low-latency small-batch profile vLLM may reduce tail spikes but might increase avg latency a bit. best to A/B with same inputs.
[13:05] Derek: ok thanks.

[END OF TRANSCRIPT]
